FerryDock / native UI comparison

Four integrations.
The same container list.

Zig + NanoUI, Go + MyGo, Rust + GPUI Kit, and Rust + gpui-pre: four small native prototypes displaying the same Docker inventory, measured on one Linux desktop.

14 real containers, frozen snapshot1,000 × 680 client pixels3 runs per integrationLinux measurementsWindows / macOS outlook belowNo automated tests added or run
Four prototypes, one shared scope. Median idle RSS is 38.23 MiB for NanoUI, 116.70 MiB for MyGo, 157.49 MiB for GPUI Kit, and 123.44 MiB for gpui-pre. The charts compare executable size, memory, and CPU. Code quality is a source-based assessment of these prototypes. Windows and macOS expectations are discussed separately from the measurements.

The direct integration removes Kit, GPUI Fast, Kit assets, and the application-level Tokio runtime. Its Linux build selects X11 and a size-oriented profile: z, fat LTO, one codegen unit, panic=abort, stripped symbols, and unwind tables disabled for compiled crates. The backend and build profile also change, so the difference does not isolate Kit's cost. No executable is compressed. Both integrations appear independently throughout this report; Kit sources, executable, and measurements are preserved in gpui-kit-baseline/.

The four apps

Actual Linux windows captured after the first run, outside the measurement interval. All four integrations also displayed the 14 containers read directly from Docker outside the measurements. Click an image to enlarge it. Screenshots preserve the prototypes' original French labels; the report itself is in English.

Shared scope: all containers; name, image, state, and status columns; search; manual Refresh; a dark theme; and virtualized rows. Logs, terminals, Docker controls, and container resource monitoring are outside this prototype. Typography and row density follow each toolkit, so the interfaces are not pixel-identical.

Code quality: a source review

Zig + NanoUI

State and ownership are explicit: a snapshot owns its arena, and the worker returns its result to the UI thread. The virtual list builds only visible rows. Toolkit components supply the text field, button, and row layout.

The implementation manually manages allocations, arena cleanup, a thread, a C callback, and filtered indices. It reads through libc popen/fread and invokes the external timeout command, introducing platform-specific work for a port.

Assessment: compact for a native Zig app, with more ownership and concurrency details to review when extending it.

Go + MyGo

The standard library covers JSON, files, and subprocess timeouts directly. A goroutine loads rows; RunOnMain publishes the result. ui.Table provides headers and virtualization. Loading, filtering, and rendering fit in one file.

Garbage collection removes manual string-lifetime management. The executable includes the Go runtime. A bounded writer caps Docker output, and a failed refresh preserves the previous inventory.

Assessment: the most direct maintenance path in these prototypes, particularly for a PHP/Node developer. This is a limited judgment about this implementation, not a conclusion about full applications.

Rust + GPUI Kit

GPUI Kit 0.8.0 with GPUI Fast 0.1.10 supplies Input, Button, and the virtualized DataTable. Application logic occupies 301 code lines in one file; text editing belongs to the library.

A GPUI worker loads data and uses a temporary Tokio runtime for the Docker subprocess, timeout, and bounded output. Sources and measurements are preserved from the archived integration.

Tradeoff: less local widget code to maintain, with a measured 42.03 MiB executable. The different backend and build profile prevent attributing the entire size gap to Kit.

Rust + gpui-pre

An independent implementation using gpui-pre 0.3.9 directly, based on Zed snapshot 93d7456. The view uses div, uniform_list, and a local search field connected to GPUI's native text input. The button is a clickable element.

GPUI's executor loads data; async-process runs Docker with bounded output and cancellation on drop. A GPUI timer enforces the timeout. There is no application polling loop.

Tradeoff: more local text editing, selection, and clipboard code. Line counts include search.rs; NanoUI, MyGo, and Kit provide their text fields through libraries. The local field has a non-blinking caret and lacks drag selection and horizontal text scrolling.

Common source-level properties: I/O runs off the UI thread, refreshes cannot overlap, output is capped at 4 MiB, the Docker command has a 10-second limit, errors remain visible, and the apps do not poll. Loading and filtering still scale with row count; virtualization limits rendering work. No automated correctness tests, audit, load profile, or accessibility verification was performed.

What this comparison measures

A short, reproducible protocol

  1. Capture docker ps --all --no-trunc --format '{{json .}}' locally, retaining the five fields used by the prototypes.
  2. All four integrations read the same 14-row NDJSON snapshot, with the same SHA-256 digest.
  3. Six initial runs alternate NanoUI and MyGo, followed by three archived Kit runs and three gpui-pre runs: twelve runs in total. Existing measurements are retained; this English/platform update did not launch new benchmarks. All builds were finished before measurement.
  4. Normalize the client surface to 1,000 × 680 pixels; use GPUI_X11_SCALE_FACTOR=1 for gpui-pre to match the observed toolkit scale. Keep the window active and pointer outside it, then allow four seconds to settle and measure twenty seconds at idle.
  5. Sample /proc every 500 ms for RSS, PSS, and CPU time of the process and its descendants.
  6. Capture the window after measurement, then close only the process group started for that run.

Limits that affect interpretation

  • CPU covers a static window at idle, not scrolling, searching, repeated refreshes, or Docker's cost.
  • RSS counts shared pages in full; PSS apportions them across processes. Neither alone covers all GPU allocations.
  • 100% CPU means one logical core. A displayed 0.00% means below the resolution of this measurement window, not proven zero work.
  • Executable size excludes dynamically loaded system libraries and the Docker CLI; it is not a self-contained package size.
  • These are warm-cache runs on a shared desktop with other applications. They do not establish a universal ranking.
  • The full FerryDock application is not measured; its scope is much broader than these minimal lists.

The backend matters as much as the language

On Linux, NanoUI renders on the CPU and presents through Cairo/GTK 3. MyGo offers GPU OpenGL rendering and a CPU fallback; an earlier diagnostic launch on this machine reported GPU rendering with MYGO_FRAME_STATS=all, outside the measured runs. Both use GTK 3 through X11/XWayland here. gpui-pre 0.3.9 uses its own X11 window and wgpu rendering; GPUI Kit uses GPUI Fast. Observed graphics libraries are retained in the raw data. MyGo loaded GLX/Mesa libraries, while NanoUI did not load OpenGL.

NanoUI describes itself as originating from a port of MyGo's core to Zig, retaining its architecture. The frameworks are related, with different feature coverage. At the pinned revision, NanoUI documents missing accessibility and several desktop APIs.

Primary sources: NanoUI platforms, NanoUI origins, MyGo native UI, gpui-pre 0.3.9.

What to expect on Windows and macOS

A portability and rendering outlook, not a benchmark. None of these four prototypes has been built, launched, or measured on Windows or macOS in this comparison. The platform entries below describe the pinned toolkits' documented backends or published source, followed by implications inferred for these apps.

Sources for the platform matrix: NanoUI platform matrix at the pinned commit; MyGo native backends at the pinned commit; GPUI Fast 0.1.10 target dependencies; gpui-pre platform selection, Windows dependencies, and Apple renderer dependencies. These establish available platform paths, not execution proof for our prototypes.

How the windows would look

Expected, not captured: the same container rows, dark palette, columns, search, and Refresh layout should remain recognizable after a port. All four use toolkit-drawn content; switching OS does not automatically replace those controls with standard Windows or AppKit widgets.

Window decorations, fonts, text rasterization, DPI scaling, and keyboard conventions can differ. On Mac, the local gpui-pre input deserves particular attention because it currently binds Ctrl-based editing shortcuts. Keeping the current dark theme would also require retaining the explicit theme choices.

No Windows/Mac screenshots or mockups are presented as real output.

How size, memory, and CPU might change

Inference: NanoUI's largest architectural change is on Mac, where its Linux CPU renderer is replaced by Metal. MyGo also switches from OpenGL to platform-specific GPU rendering. Both GPUI variants use target-specific graphics and text dependencies. Idle fixed costs, active rendering costs, and executable contents can therefore change.

The 14-row workload is small, so framework, font, window, and driver overhead can outweigh the data itself. No justified Windows/Mac MiB estimate or ordering follows from the Linux results. Apple Silicon and x86-64 builds also differ; a universal Mac executable includes more than one architecture.

GPU rendering alone does not guarantee lower idle RAM or CPU. The measured Linux ranking must be remeasured on each target.

What a fair follow-up would measure. Build release executables for each target, run the same JSON snapshot and display size, and report executable size separately from installers, app bundles, and debug symbols. Keep Docker engine/VM consumption outside UI memory figures; the snapshot already avoids that dependency during sampling. Windows working-set measures and macOS memory/footprint measures do not map exactly to Linux RSS/PSS, so record each metric explicitly. Then observe live Docker loading and the native text field separately. No cross-platform run or port is included in the current work.
